mainTopic: Suspect litigants, the oaths of those who swear and collect, and why the רבנן let a hired worker swear and collect his wages.
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about oaths and begins the גמרא. A person who swore falsely is suspect about oaths. So are people who take money unfairly, like dice players and lenders with interest. When one side is suspect, the other side swears and collects. If both are suspect, רבי יוסי and רבי מאיר disagree about what happens. The משנה then explains the storekeeper's ledger case, where בן ננס objects to letting two people swear opposite things. Next come disputes between a customer and a storekeeper or money changer, where רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion. The משנה then lists cases where a woman collects her כתובה, or orphans collect a debt, only with an oath. It ends with people who must swear even without a specific claim. In the גמרא, a פסוק shows that Torah oaths only free a person from paying. The גמרא then works hard to explain why the רבנן let a hired worker swear and collect. Its final answer is that the busy employer probably forgot to pay, and the oath puts his mind at ease.

steps.title: Any false oath makes a person suspect
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states that someone who swore falsely becomes suspect about oaths. This applies whether it was a שבועת העדות, a שבועת הפקדון, or even a שבועת שוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes no difference whether it was an oath about testimony or an oath about a deposit, or even a pointless oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is finishing its definition of a חשוד על השבועה. Any of these false oaths puts a person in that category.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think only a serious false oath, one that cheats someone out of money, makes a person untrustworthy. The word ואפילו teaches that even a שבועת שוא counts. Once he swore falsely in any of these ways, the court will not let him swear.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath by a witness that he knows no testimony
An oath denying that one holds someone's deposit or money
A vain oath, such as swearing that something obviously true is true
A person suspected regarding oaths, whom the court does not let swear

phrases.english: Whether it was an oath of testimony
or an oath about a deposit,
or even a vain oath;

steps.triggerLanguage: אַחַת שְׁבוּעַת הָעֵדוּת וְאַחַת שְׁבוּעַת הַפִּקָּדוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's discussion of a litigant who is suspect about oaths.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Swearing falsely with any kind of oath, even a שבועת שוא, makes a person a חשוד על השבועה.

steps.title: Rabbinic categories of suspect people, and the other side swears
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists people the חכמים treat as suspect: a dice player, a lender with interest, pigeon flyers, and traders in שביעית produce. When one litigant is like this, the other litigant swears and collects.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one of the two sides was a dice player, a lender with interest, a pigeon flyer, or a seller of שביעית produce, the other side swears and takes the money.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists people who are untrustworthy with oaths because of how they live. It rules that the oath shifts to the other side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These people never swore falsely in court. But they regularly take money that is not really theirs, so the חכמים assume they would also swear falsely. Normally the defendant swears and goes free. Here the defendant cannot swear, so the claimant swears and collects.

keyTerms.meaning: One who plays dice for money
One who lends money with interest
Those who race or fly pigeons for bets
Those who trade in produce of the שמיטה year

steps.confusionAlert: 'The one opposite him swears and takes' means the honest side now takes the oath. The suspect person is not punished. He simply loses the chance to swear.

phrases.english: If one of them was a dice player,
phrases.notes: 'One of them' means one of the two sides in the court case.

phrases.english: or one who lends with interest,
or among those who fly pigeons,
or among traders in Sabbatical-year produce
then the one opposite him swears and takes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds rabbinic categories of suspect people to the biblical ones in step 1, and gives the ruling for when one side is suspect.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When one litigant is suspect about oaths, the opposing litigant swears and collects.

steps.title: Both sides suspect: רבי יוסי says the oath returns to its place
steps.stepSummary: If both litigants are suspect, רבי יוסי rules that 'the oath returns to its place.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If both of them were suspect, the oath goes back to where it started. These are the words of רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now handles the case where neither side can be trusted to swear. רבי יוסי gives his ruling, and the גמרא will later explain what it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 2 the oath could move to the honest side. Here there is no honest side to move it to. רבי יוסי's short phrase 'returns to its place' is not explained in the משנה itself.

keyTerms.meaning: The oath returns to its place

phrases.english: If both of them were suspect,
the oath returns to its place,
these are the words of Rabbi Yosei.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from one suspect litigant to two suspect litigants.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יוסי, when both are suspect the oath returns to its place.

steps.title: רבי מאיר says they split the money
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר disagrees with רבי יוסי. When both sides are suspect, they divide the disputed money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: they should split it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר gives a different ruling for the same case. Since nobody can swear, the two sides share the money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a מחלוקת with רבי יוסי from step 3. רבי מאיר does not try to settle the case with an oath at all. Splitting is a compromise when neither claim can be confirmed.
steps.whatToRemember: One suspect side: the other side swears and collects. Both sides suspect: רבי יוסי says the oath returns to its place, and רבי מאיר says they split.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: they divide it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion to רבי יוסי on the same case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, when both are suspect they divide the disputed amount.

steps.title: How does the storekeeper's ledger case work?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה returns to the storekeeper with his ledger, one of the people who 'swear and collect,' and asks what exact case it means.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the storekeeper relying on his ledger: what case is that?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks a clarifying question to set up its explanation of the storekeeper case. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the פרק, the storekeeper was listed among those who swear and collect. The משנה now asks for the exact situation, because a storekeeper does not collect on a ledger entry in every case.

phrases.english: And the storekeeper on his ledger: how is that?
phrases.notes: This points back to the earlier list in this פרק of people who swear and collect, where the storekeeper appeared.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of suspect litigants and returns to define the storekeeper case from earlier in the פרק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact situation in which a storekeeper swears and collects based on his ledger.

steps.title: The case: the customer sent his son or workers to the storekeeper
steps.stepSummary: The ruling does not cover a storekeeper who just says 'my ledger says you owe me.' It covers a customer who told the storekeeper to give his son wheat or his workers coins. The storekeeper says he gave, the workers say they received nothing, and both swear and collect from the customer.
steps.simpleTranslation: It does not mean he says to him: 'It is written in my ledger that you owe me 200 זוז.' Rather, the customer said to him: 'Give my son two סאה of wheat' or 'Give my workers a סלע's worth of coins.' The storekeeper says, 'I gave,' and they say, 'We did not get it.' He swears and collects, and they swear and collect.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers its question by describing the exact case. The customer agrees he gave the order, and the only question is whether the storekeeper actually paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain ledger entry is not enough to make a customer pay. Here the customer admits he sent the storekeeper to pay on his behalf, so he owes someone. The storekeeper has an argument from his ledger, and the workers have an argument for their wages. Each one swears, and the customer pays both.

keyTerms.meaning: Two סאה, a measure of grain

steps.confusionAlert: Both the storekeeper and the workers collect from the customer who sent them, not from each other. That is why the customer can end up paying twice.
steps.whyThisMatters: Because the customer pays twice, and one of the two oaths must be false, this case sets up בן ננס's objection.

phrases.english: Not where he says to him:
'It is written in my ledger
that you owe me two hundred zuz,'
rather, where he says to him:
phrases.notes: Now the customer is speaking to the storekeeper.

phrases.english: 'Give my son two se'ah of wheat,'
'Give my workers small coins for a sela.'
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, 'for a סלע,' meaning small change worth one סלע.

phrases.english: He says, 'I gave,'
and they say, 'We did not receive':
he swears and collects,
and they swear and collect.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שֶׁיֹּאמַר לוֹ כְּתוֹב עַל פִּנְקָסִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case is where the customer admits he told the storekeeper to pay his son or workers. Then both the storekeeper and the workers swear and collect from the customer.

steps.title: בן ננס: how can we let both sides swear?
steps.stepSummary: בן ננס objects that the storekeeper and the workers say opposite things, so one of them must be swearing falsely.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן ננס said: How can we bring both of these people to a false oath?
steps.whatsHappening: בן ננס challenges the ruling of step 6. The court would be causing one person to swear falsely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The storekeeper says 'I paid,' and the workers say 'we were not paid.' Both cannot be true. Letting both swear means the court knowingly allows a שבועת שוא.

keyTerms.meaning: These and those, meaning both sides

phrases.english: Ben Nannas said:
How can both these and those
come to a vain oath?

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד אֵלּוּ וְאֵלּוּ בָּאִין לִידֵי שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling of step 6 that both parties swear.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that both the storekeeper and the workers swear and collect.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Their claims contradict, so one oath is certainly false. A court should not set up a guaranteed false oath.

steps.title: בן ננס's ruling: both collect without an oath
steps.stepSummary: בן ננס rules that the storekeeper and the workers each collect from the customer, but without swearing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he collects without an oath, and they collect without an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: בן ננס gives his own ruling to avoid the problem he raised. Both sides still get paid, but nobody swears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן ננס keeps the result that the customer pays both. He only removes the oaths, so no false oath happens. The customer is still responsible for both, because he is the one who sent the storekeeper to pay.
steps.whatToRemember: The first view (תנא קמא): the storekeeper and the workers both swear and collect from the customer. בן ננס: both collect from him without swearing, so that no one comes to a false oath.

phrases.english: Rather, he collects without an oath,
and they collect without an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives בן ננס's alternative ruling after his objection in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to בן ננס, the storekeeper and the workers each collect from the customer without an oath.

steps.title: Customer claims he already paid the storekeeper
steps.stepSummary: A customer got produce worth a dinar. The storekeeper asks for the dinar, and the customer says he already paid. The customer swears that he paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: A customer told a storekeeper, 'Give me a dinar's worth of produce,' and the storekeeper gave it. Then the storekeeper said, 'Give me that dinar.' The customer said, 'I gave it to you, and you put it in your wallet.' The customer swears that he paid the dinar.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens a new case: a customer and a storekeeper argue about whether the customer paid for produce he received. The customer swears that he paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree the produce was handed over. The only question is whether the dinar was paid. Here the customer is the one who takes the oath, and after he swears he does not have to pay again.

keyTerms.meaning: A silver coin of a set value

phrases.english: He said to a storekeeper: "Give me produce for a dinar,"
and he gave it to him.
The storekeeper said to him: "Give me that dinar,"
He said to him: "I gave it to you, and you put it in your wallet"

phrases.aramaic: – יִשָּׁבַע בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁנָּתַן לוֹ אֶת הַדִּינָר.
phrases.english: The customer swears that he gave him the dinar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new set of storekeeper cases in the משנה. These are separate from the ledger case in steps 5-8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a customer claims he paid for produce he received, the customer swears that he paid.

steps.title: Storekeeper claims he already gave the produce
steps.stepSummary: The customer paid the dinar and asks for the produce. The storekeeper says he already delivered it. The storekeeper swears.
steps.simpleTranslation: The customer paid and said, 'Give me the produce.' The storekeeper said, 'I gave it to you, and it was carried into your house.' The storekeeper swears.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה flips the case. Now the payment is agreed, and the argument is about whether the produce was delivered. The storekeeper swears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mirrors step 9. The person who claims he already did his part is the one who swears. Here that is the storekeeper, so after his oath he does not have to give the produce again.

phrases.english: The customer said to him: "Give me the produce,"

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: ״נְתַתִּים לָךְ וְהוֹלַכְתִּים לְתוֹךְ בֵּיתְךָ״
phrases.english: He said to him: "I gave it to you, and it was carried into your house"
phrases.notes: The Hebrew can also be read 'I carried them.' Either way, he's saying the produce already got to the customer's house.

phrases.english: The storekeeper swears.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reverse case of step 9: the payment is agreed, and the delivery is disputed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a storekeeper claims he already delivered paid-for produce, the storekeeper swears.

steps.title: Whoever holds the produce has the upper hand
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that whoever is holding the produce wins the argument.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Whoever has the produce in his hands has the upper hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the ruling before him. He says the person holding the produce is believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion always required an oath. רבי יהודה instead looks at who actually has the produce now. That person wins, and his claim is accepted without an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: His hand is on top: he has the advantage

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Whoever has the produce in his hand,
his hand is on top.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: כׇּל שֶׁהַפֵּירוֹת בְּיָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A disagreeing opinion on the storekeeper cases in steps 9-10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever is holding the produce is believed.

steps.title: The same two cases with a money changer
steps.stepSummary: The same pattern repeats with a money changer who gives small coins for a dinar. If the dinar is disputed, the customer swears. If the coins are disputed, the money changer swears.
steps.simpleTranslation: A customer told a money changer, 'Give me small coins for a dinar,' and he gave them. The money changer said, 'Give me the dinar.' The customer said, 'I gave it to you, and you put it in your wallet.' The customer swears. In the other case, the customer gave the dinar and said, 'Give me the coins.' The money changer said, 'I gave them to you, and you threw them into your purse.' The money changer swears.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה repeats both storekeeper cases, this time with a money changer. The outcome is the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like with the storekeeper, the person who says he already handed over his side is the one who swears. The משנה repeats the rule for money changers to set up רבי יהודה's comment in the next step, which depends on how money changers usually work.

phrases.english: He said to a money changer: "Give me small coins for a dinar,"
and he gave them to him.
The money changer said to him: "Give me the dinar,"
He said to him: "I gave it to you, and you put it in your wallet"
The customer swears.
If he gave him the dinar,
and said to him: "Give me the coins,"

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: ״נְתַתִּים לָךְ וְהִשְׁלַכְתָּ לְתוֹךְ כִּיסְךָ״ –
phrases.english: and he said to him: "I gave them to you, and you threw them into your purse"
The money changer swears.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same two rulings from steps 9-10 to a money changer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the dinar is disputed, the customer swears. If the coins are disputed, the money changer swears.

steps.title: A money changer never hands over coins before being paid
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says a money changer does not give even a small coin until he has received the dinar.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: A money changer does not normally give even an איסר until he has taken the dinar.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees again. This time he points to how money changers normally do business.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Money changers are careful to take payment first. So if the customer already has the coins, we assume the money changer was paid. That means the customer is believed in the first case.

keyTerms.meaning: A small coin of low value

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
It is not a money changer's way to give an issar
until he takes a dinar.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֵין דֶּרֶךְ שׁוּלְחָנִי לִיתֵּן אִיסָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A disagreeing opinion on the money changer cases in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A money changer does not give coins before he is paid, so a customer who has the coins is assumed to have paid.
steps.whatToRemember: In all four cases, the first opinion says the person who claims he already handed over his side swears. רבי יהודה instead looks at who holds the goods, or at what usually happens.

steps.title: Cases where a woman collects her כתובה only with an oath
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists situations where a woman can collect her כתובה only after taking an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as the חכמים said: A woman who lowers the value of her כתובה collects only with an oath. If one witness says it was paid, she collects only with an oath. From sold property or from orphans' property, she collects only with an oath. And a woman who collects when he is not present collects only with an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה compares the earlier oath cases to a list of known cases where a woman may collect her כתובה only after swearing. The phrase "כשם שאמרו" sets up this list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In each case there is some doubt about whether she is still owed the full amount. She may have admitted to a partial payment, one witness may say she was paid, the property may now belong to buyers or orphans, or the husband is not there to answer. In all of these, she must swear before she collects.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who lowers the value of her כתובה by admitting she got part of it
Property that was tied to the debt and later sold to others

phrases.english: Just as they said:
A woman who lowers the value of her marriage contract
collects only with an oath.
And if one witness testifies that it was paid,
she collects only with an oath.
From liened property and from orphans' property,
she collects only with an oath.
And one who collects not in his presence
phrases.notes: "His" means her husband: she is collecting while he is not there to argue back.

phrases.english: collects only with an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links the oath cases of the פרק to a known list of people who collect only with an oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman collects her כתובה only with an oath in four situations: she lowered its value, one witness says it was paid, she collects from sold or orphans' property, or her husband is not present.

steps.title: Orphans collect their father's debt only with an oath
steps.stepSummary: Orphans who collect a loan owed to their father must first swear that, as far as they know, the debt was not paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: And likewise, orphans collect only with an oath: 'We swear that our father did not instruct us, and our father did not tell us, and we did not find among our father's documents, that this document was paid.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds orphans to the list of people who collect only with an oath. It also gives the exact wording of their oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Orphans cannot know for sure whether the loan was repaid to their father. So they swear only about what they know: they got no instruction, heard nothing, and found no record that it was paid.

keyTerms.meaning: A written document, here a loan document

phrases.english: And likewise, the orphans
collect only with an oath:
"An oath that our father did not instruct us,
and our father did not tell us,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא מָצִינוּ בֵּין שְׁטָרוֹתָיו שֶׁל אַבָּא
phrases.english: and that we did not find among our father's documents
that this document was paid."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הַיְּתוֹמִים – לֹא יִפָּרְעוּ אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds orphans to the list of people in step 14 who collect only with an oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Orphans collect their father's debt only after swearing they know of no sign that it was paid.

steps.title: Even a son born after his father died swears
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה says that even a son born after his father's death swears and collects.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה says: Even if the son was born after the father died, he swears and collects.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה adds to the orphans' rule. He applies it even to a son who never knew his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Such a son obviously never heard anything from his father. Still, he must take the oath, because it also covers what he might have found among his father's documents.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka says:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ נוֹלַד הַבֵּן לְאַחַר מִיתַת הָאָב –
phrases.english: Even if the son was born after the father's death,
he swears and collects.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ נוֹלַד הַבֵּן לְאַחַר מִיתַת הָאָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the orphans' oath in step 15 to a son born after his father's death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A son born after his father's death still swears in order to collect his father's debt.

steps.title: No oath if the father declared the loan unpaid
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that if witnesses heard the father say before he died that the loan was not paid, the son collects without an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: If there are witnesses that the father said at the time of his death, 'This document is not paid,' the son collects without an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל gives an exception to the orphans' oath. If there are witnesses to the father's statement, no oath is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath is there to remove doubt about whether the loan was repaid. If witnesses heard the father say at his death that it was still unpaid, that doubt is gone, so the son collects without swearing.

keyTerms.meaning: At the time of his death

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ עֵדִים שֶׁאָמַר הָאָב בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ:
phrases.english: If there are witnesses that the father said at the time of his death:
"This document is not paid,"
he collects without an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: אִם יֵשׁ עֵדִים שֶׁאָמַר הָאָב בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception to the orphans' oath from step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If witnesses heard the father say at his death that the loan was unpaid, the son collects without an oath.
steps.whatToRemember: Orphans normally swear before collecting their father's debt, even a son born after his father died. But if witnesses heard the father say the loan was unpaid, no oath is needed.

steps.title: People who swear even without a specific claim
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists people who manage someone else's property: partners, sharecroppers, guardians, a woman running the household business, and a household manager. They can be made to swear even when no specific claim is made against them.
steps.simpleTranslation: These people swear even without a claim: partners, sharecroppers, guardians, a woman who does business inside the house, and a household manager. If one says, 'What are you claiming from me?' and the other answers, 'I just want you to swear to me,' he must swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new list. These are people who can be made to take an oath even though the other side has no definite claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person only swears when there is a real claim against him. These people handle another person's money with a lot of freedom, so the owner may suspect them without being able to point to anything specific. The משנה says 'I just want you to swear' is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: without a claim, with no specific accusation
sharecroppers who work a field for a share of the crop
guardians or stewards managing someone else's property
a household member put in charge of the home's affairs

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think these people are being accused of stealing. The whole point is that there is no specific accusation, yet they still must swear.

phrases.english: And these swear even without a claim:
partners, sharecroppers, and guardians,
and the woman who does business inside the house,
phrases.notes: Literally 'who carries and gives': she buys and sells for the household.

phrases.english: and the household manager.
If he said to him: 'What are you claiming from me?'
and the other answered, 'I want you to swear to me,' he is obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the list of people who swear and collect to a new list of people who swear without a claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partners, sharecroppers, guardians, a woman running household business, and a household manager must swear on demand, even with no specific claim.

steps.title: Limits on the oath: after dividing, carrying over, and שביעית
steps.stepSummary: Once partners or sharecroppers divide, the other side can no longer make them swear without a claim. If an oath comes up from another matter, though, every other issue can be added onto it. שביעית cancels the oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the partners or sharecroppers already divided, one cannot make the other swear. If he becomes obligated in an oath from some other matter, they can add everything onto that oath. And שביעית cancels the oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives three limits or extensions to the rule from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the partnership ends, the special oath without a claim ends too. But if a real oath is required for something else, the other side may 'roll' all its suspicions onto that same oath, which is called גלגול שבועה. A debt oath is also canceled by שביעית, just like the debt itself.

keyTerms.meaning: they divided (the shared property), ending the partnership
'rolling over' an oath: adding other issues onto an oath someone already owes
the seventh (שמיטה) year, which cancels debts

steps.whatToRemember: There are three points here. Once partners divide, the oath without a claim stops. An oath owed for one matter can carry other issues with it (גלגול). שביעית cancels the oath along with the debt.

phrases.english: If the partners or sharecroppers divided,
he cannot make him swear.
If an oath came upon him from some other matter,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some have the corrected word in square brackets. Both mean 'came rolling onto him'.

phrases.english: they may roll everything onto him.
And the seventh year cancels the oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets limits and extensions on the oath without a claim from step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After dividing, no oath without a claim can be imposed. An oath from another matter can carry everything with it. שביעית cancels the oath.

steps.title: Where do we learn that Torah oaths free a person from paying?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by quoting the משנה's rule that people who swear by Torah law swear and do not pay. It asks where this comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: All who swear by Torah law swear and do not pay. From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins. It quotes the first rule of the משנה and asks for its source, setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule says that a Torah oath is always taken by the one who would otherwise pay, and the oath frees him. The גמרא wants a פסוק that teaches this.

keyTerms.meaning: the start of the גמרא's discussion
they swear and do not pay
from where do we know this?

phrases.english: GEMARA: All who swear by Torah law
swear and do not pay.
From where do we know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The משנה has ended; the גמרא goes back to the first line of the משנה to find its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Torah source showing that Torah oaths free the swearer from paying.

steps.title: The פסוק: the one who would pay is the one who swears
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says the owner accepts the oath 'and he shall not pay.' So the oath goes to the one who would otherwise have to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And its owner shall accept, and he shall not pay.' The one who would have to pay is the one who gets the oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק from the laws of a guardian (שומר).
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'and he shall not pay' come right after the oath. This shows the oath is what frees the swearer from paying. So in the Torah, the oath always belongs to the one facing payment.
steps.whatToRemember: A Torah oath frees the swearer from paying. It never lets him collect.

phrases.english: Because the verse says:
'And its owner shall accept, and he shall not pay.'
The one who would have to pay,
to him goes the oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the מנלן of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שמות 22:10, 'and he shall not pay', shows the oath goes to the one who would otherwise pay and frees him.

steps.title: Why does the hired worker get to swear and collect?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's list of people who swear and collect. It asks why the רבנן made such a rule for a hired worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And these swear and take' and so on. What is different about a hired worker, that the רבנן set up for him that he swears and takes?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next part of the משנה and asks why a hired worker gets a special rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We just learned that a Torah oath only frees a person from paying. Here the worker swears in order to collect, which is the opposite. So this must be a rule of the רבנן, and the גמרא wants to know why they gave it to him.

phrases.english: 'And these swear and take,' and so on.
What is different about a hired worker
that the Rabbis instituted for him
that he swears and takes?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After showing that Torah oaths only free a person from paying, the גמרא asks about a rabbinic oath that lets someone collect.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the Rabbis gave the hired worker an oath that lets him collect.

steps.title: שמואל: great הלכות were taught here
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reports in the name of שמואל that 'great הלכות' were taught in this משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: Great הלכות were taught here.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל responds that this part of the משנה contains major rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל calls the oaths that let people collect especially important rulings. He is pointing out that these are big, special rules, not ordinary ones.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
Great laws were taught here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the question about the hired worker.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: These oaths are major, special rulings.

steps.title: Are these really 'הלכות'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to שמואל's word 'הלכות'. These oaths are rabbinic, not הלכות in the full sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'הלכות'? Are these really הלכות?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the word שמואל used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'הלכה' usually means a law handed down from סיני (הלכה למשה מסיני). We just saw that the Rabbis made these rules, so calling them 'הלכות' seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: a law, often meaning one handed down from סיני

phrases.english: 'Laws'? Are these really laws?!
phrases.notes: These oaths were set up by the Rabbis, so the word 'laws' doesn't fit them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of שמואל's statement in step 23.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'הלכות' suggests law from סיני, but step 22 established these oaths are a rabbinic enactment.

steps.title: Correct it to 'great תקנות'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes שמואל's wording to 'great תקנות were taught here', meaning major rabbinic enactments.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: Great enactments were taught here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording so it fits a rabbinic rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'תקנות', שמואל's point becomes accurate. The oaths that let people collect, like the hired worker's, are major enactments of the Rabbis. The idea stays the same; only the label changes.

keyTerms.meaning: rather, say (a correction of the wording)

steps.whatToRemember: The hired worker's oath to collect is a major rabbinic תקנה, not a Torah law.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
Great enactments were taught here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the wording challenge of step 24.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל called these oaths 'הלכות', which sounds like law from סיני.
steps.terutzMaskana: The statement should read 'תקנות גדולות': these oaths are major rabbinic enactments.

steps.title: Does 'great' imply some enactments are small?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the word 'great' in the corrected wording of שמואל's statement.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Great' תקנות? That implies there are also small ones!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the fixed version of שמואל's statement from the last step. Calling these תקנות 'great' sounds as if other rabbinic enactments are small.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 25 the word 'הלכות' was changed to 'תקנות' to fix the first problem. Now the adjective 'great' is attacked. Every enactment of the רבנן carries full weight, so none should be described as 'small'.

phrases.english: 'Great' [enactments]?
This implies that there are small ones!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording 'great תקנות' that Step 25 had just proposed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'great תקנות' in the corrected version of שמואל's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Describing some תקנות as 'great' implies that others are small, which is not acceptable.

steps.title: Fixed enactments: the oath moved to the worker for his livelihood
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of שמואל says these are 'fixed תקנות'. The רבנן moved the שבועה from the בעל הבית to the שכיר because his wages are his livelihood.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: Fixed enactments were taught here. The רבנן uprooted the oath from the employer and placed it on the hired worker, because his wages are his livelihood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the word 'great' and brings a different version of שמואל's statement: 'fixed תקנות.' It also gives the reason for the rule: the worker lives on his wages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law the בעל הבית would swear and not pay, as Step 21 showed. The רבנן switched it so the שכיר swears and collects. The reason given here is that the worker depends on these wages to live.

keyTerms.meaning: his livelihood (literally: enough for his life)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic statement of the תקנה: a rabbinic change that moves the שבועה from one side to the other. The rest of the passage tests its reason.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Naḥman said that Shmuel said:
Fixed enactments were taught here:
The Rabbis uprooted the oath from the employer
and placed it on the hired worker,
because of his livelihood.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected wording with a new version of שמואל's statement and adds a reason.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל called them 'fixed תקנות', and the reason is the worker's livelihood.

steps.title: Why should the employer lose out for the worker?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the בעל הבית should be penalized just to protect the שכיר's livelihood.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of the hired worker's livelihood, we penalize the employer?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason just given. Protecting one person should not mean taking away the rights of the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving the שבועה to the worker leaves the employer open to a dishonest worker who swears falsely and collects twice. Why should the רבנן favor one side at the other's cost?

phrases.english: Because of the livelihood of the hired worker,
do we penalize the employer?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם כְּדֵי חַיָּיו דְּשָׂכִיר קָנְסִינַן לֵיהּ לְבַעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in Step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The livelihood reason for moving the שבועה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The worker's need does not explain why the employer should lose his Torah-given right to swear and be free.

steps.title: The employer also gains, since workers will agree to work for him
steps.stepSummary: The בעל הבית himself wants the שכיר to swear and collect, so that workers will be willing to work for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The employer himself is happy for the worker to swear and collect, so that workers will agree to be hired by him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the employer is not really being penalized. The rule helps him too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If workers feared they could lose their wages, they would avoid working for him. Because the rule protects workers, employers can find workers easily. So the תקנה is good for both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: it is comfortable for him, he prefers

phrases.english: The employer himself prefers
that the hired worker swears and collects,
so that workers will agree to be hired by him.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean roughly the same thing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 28 by showing that the employer benefits too.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a hidden benefit to the side that seems to lose
steps.terutzMaskana: The employer gains, because workers will be willing to work for him.

steps.title: The worker could gain from the opposite rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the argument around. The שכיר would also gain if the בעל הבית swore and was free, because then employers would hire him readily.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! The worker should prefer that the employer swears and is freed, so that the employer will hire him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the same kind of reasoning against the answer. If 'it helps the other side too' is a good argument, it works just as well for the Torah's original rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the Torah rule the employer is protected, so employers would feel safe hiring. That helps workers find jobs. So the benefit argument does not prove which side should swear.

phrases.english: On the contrary, the hired worker should prefer
that the employer swears and is released,
so that the employer will hire him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the reasoning of Step 29 around.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the employer benefits from the תקנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same 'benefit' logic supports the Torah rule just as well, so it cannot be the reason for the change.

steps.title: The employer has no choice but to hire
steps.stepSummary: The בעל הבית must hire workers anyway, so the worker gains nothing by protecting him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The employer hires against his will.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the employer needs his work done, so he will hire workers no matter what the rule is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the employer will hire anyway, the worker does not need to win him over by letting him swear. The benefit only goes one way: workers need protection to agree to work.

keyTerms.meaning: against his will, he has no choice

phrases.english: The employer hires against his will.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 30 by showing the employer's need is unavoidable.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the two sides are not equal
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The worker would gain from the employer being protected.
steps.terutzMaskana: The employer must hire anyway, so the worker gains nothing from that.

steps.title: The worker also has no choice
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers back that the שכיר also must take work, since he needs to make a living.
steps.simpleTranslation: The hired worker is also hired against his will!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the last answer. The worker needs a job just as much as the employer needs workers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both sides are forced to deal with each other, neither one needs a special benefit to come to the table. That knocks out the whole 'benefit' line of reasoning.

phrases.english: The hired worker is also hired against his will!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects Step 31 by applying the same logic to the worker.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the employer hires out of need.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The worker takes work out of need too, so the two sides are equal and the benefit argument fails.

steps.title: New reason: the employer is busy with his workers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the 'benefit' approach. The real reason is that the בעל הבית is busy with many workers and may forget whether he paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the employer is busy with his workers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a completely new reason for the תקנה. The employer has many workers to deal with, so his memory of paying is less reliable than the worker's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker has only one employer and one wage to remember. The employer may mix up who he paid. So it makes sense to trust the worker's שבועה over the employer's.
steps.whatToRemember: The final reason the שכיר swears and collects: the בעל הבית is busy with many workers and may have forgotten, while the worker remembers his own pay.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying the employer is lying. It only says that an honest but busy employer could easily make a mistake.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בַּעַל הַבַּיִת טָרוּד בְּפוֹעֲלָיו הוּא.
phrases.english: Rather, the employer is busy with his workers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בַּעַל הַבַּיִת טָרוּד בְּפוֹעֲלָיו הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Drops the failed benefit reasoning and gives a new reason for the תקנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reason replacing the failed one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תקנה exists because each side benefits.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תקנה exists because the busy employer probably forgot, so the worker is believed with a שבועה.

steps.title: Then pay him without any oath
steps.stepSummary: If the employer probably forgot, the גמרא asks why the שכיר should need a שבועה at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let him give him [the wages] without an oath!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reason. This sets up the next answer, which comes in the following step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we assume the employer forgot, the worker's claim looks true, so why make him swear? The גמרא must explain why a שבועה is still needed.

phrases.english: Then let him give him [the wages] without an oath!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'busy employer' reason from Step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the worker's שבועה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the employer most likely forgot, the worker's claim should be accepted with no שבועה at all.

steps.title: The oath calms the employer's mind
steps.stepSummary: The שכיר swears so that the בעל הבית, who may have forgotten, can feel sure he is not being cheated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The oath is there to put the employer's mind at ease.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 34: if the employer probably forgot, why does the שכיר need a שבועה? It is to calm the בעל הבית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We assume the busy employer probably forgot, so the worker collects. Still, the employer may worry he is being cheated, so the worker must take a שבועה first. That way the employer can trust he is not paying twice.

keyTerms.meaning: to put his mind at ease, to settle his worry
the employer, the owner who hired the worker

phrases.english: In order to put the mind at ease
phrases.notes: This answers the last question: why the worker must swear if the employer probably just forgot.

phrases.english: of the employer.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדֵי לְהָפִיס דַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 34
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the purpose of the oath
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the employer forgot, the worker should collect with no oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: The worker swears so the employer can be calm that he is not being cheated.

steps.title: Why not pay in front of witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why חכמים did not tell the employer to pay in front of עדים, so no oath would be needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him pay the worker in front of witnesses!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a simpler fix: the בעל הבית should pay with עדים watching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there were עדים, there would be no doubt about whether he paid. So why do we need a שבועה at all? The גמרא is pushing on whether the oath system is really needed.

keyTerms.meaning: and let him give him (pay him)

phrases.english: But let him give it to him in front of witnesses!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the oath given in Step 35
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the שבועה to settle the employer's mind
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Paying in front of עדים would remove the doubt, so no oath would be needed.

steps.title: Witnesses are too much trouble
steps.stepSummary: Finding עדים every time he pays would be a burden for the employer.
steps.simpleTranslation: That would be a bother for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that bringing עדים every time he pays wages is too much trouble.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An employer pays many workers often. Having to find עדים each time is not practical. So חכמים did not require it.

keyTerms.meaning: the matter is a bother for him

phrases.english: The matter is a bother for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 36
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Paying with עדים would be an easy fix.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is too burdensome, so the oath system is used instead.

steps.title: Why not pay at the start?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the employer does not simply pay when he hires the worker, so there is never a doubt later.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him pay the worker right at the beginning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another fix: pay up front, when the job begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the money is given at the start, there is nothing to forget at the end of the day. Then there would be no argument and no need for a שבועה.

keyTerms.meaning: from the start, at the beginning

phrases.english: But let him give it to him at the start!
phrases.notes: He means pay the wages when he hires the worker, before the work is done.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge after the witness idea was rejected
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Paying up front would remove any later doubt, so no oath would be needed.

steps.title: Both sides prefer paying later
steps.stepSummary: Both the employer and the worker want payment to come after the work, on credit (הקפה).
steps.simpleTranslation: Both of them want it on credit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that neither side wants payment up front. Both prefer that the money comes later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בעל הבית may not have money ready when he hires. The worker also prefers to get his pay at the end. Since paying later is what both want, the doubt can come up, and the שבועה is the fix.

keyTerms.meaning: credit, paying later instead of right away

steps.whatToRemember: The שכיר swears and collects to calm the בעל הבית. Other fixes don't work: עדים are too much trouble, and both sides want to pay later (הקפה).

phrases.english: Both of them want it on credit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 38
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Paying at the start would solve everything.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sides want payment later, so the oath system stays.
